items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What is the broadcast address of the subnet that GigabitEthernet0/1 belongs to?

exhibit.content:
! R1 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 description accounting LAN
 ip address 192.168.20.100 255.255.255.224
 no shutdown
!

items.explanation: A 255.255.255.224 mask is a /27, so subnets step in blocks of 32 and .100 falls in the block running from .96 to .127; the last address, .127, is the broadcast. Option B is the network address of the next subnet, an error of exactly one address past the boundary. Option C is the broadcast for the whole /24 and ignores that the interface is subnetted at all. Option D is the last usable host address, which sits one below the broadcast.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why does PC1 get no reply from PC2 even though both are cabled to the same switch?

exhibit.content:
! Two hosts on one switched segment, no router present
!
PC1   IPv4 address . . . : 192.168.10.70
      Subnet mask  . . . : 255.255.255.192

PC2   IPv4 address . . . : 192.168.10.130
      Subnet mask  . . . : 255.255.255.192

PC1 can reach 192.168.10.65 but gets no reply from PC2.

options.text: 192.168.10.130 is the broadcast address of the subnet PC1 occupies.
PC2's address lies outside the private range and requires translation.
The /26 mask places the two hosts in different subnets.
Both hosts resolve to the same network address, so their addresses conflict.

items.explanation: 255.255.255.192 is a /26, giving blocks of 64: PC1's .70 sits in the .64 to .127 subnet while PC2's .130 sits in .128 to .191, so the two need a router between them despite sharing a switch. That PC1 reaches .65 confirms its own subnet works. Option A is wrong because the broadcast of PC1's subnet is .127. Option B misapplies private addressing, since all of 192.168.0.0/16 is private. Option D describes an address conflict, which would need the two hosts to share one address.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which set of subnets satisfies every host requirement without overlapping?

exhibit.content:
Address block available for the branch:  172.16.8.0/22

    Segment            Hosts required
    ---------------    --------------
    User LAN                      500
    Voice LAN                     200
    Server LAN                    100
    Management LAN                 50

The four segments must be carved from the block with no overlap.

items.explanation: Each segment needs the smallest subnet that still fits it: 500 hosts need a /23 giving 510, 200 need a /24 giving 254, 100 need a /25 giving 126, and 50 need a /26 giving 62. Placed in descending order from 172.16.8.0 those four tile the /22 exactly. Option A starts with a /24, which offers only 254 addresses and cannot hold 500 hosts. Option B opens with the entire /22, leaving nothing for the other three. Option C assigns a /24 at 172.16.11.0 that swallows the /26 placed at 172.16.11.128.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which address in this subnet cannot be assigned to a host?

exhibit.content:
! R4 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.10.10.65 255.255.255.192
 no shutdown
!

items.explanation: The 255.255.255.192 mask is a /26, so the interface sits in the block from 10.10.10.64 to 10.10.10.127; the last address is the broadcast and is unusable, leaving .65 through .126 for hosts. Option A is the highest usable host address, one below the broadcast. Option C sits comfortably inside the usable range. Option D is the router's own configured address, which is a perfectly ordinary host address and is shown in the exhibit already in use.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which subnet mask meets the host requirement while producing the largest number of subnets?

exhibit.content:
192.168.5.0/24
        +---------+---------+---------+---------+
            |           |         |         |
        +---+---+   +---+---+ +---+---+ +---+---+
        | Sales |   |Support| |Finance| |  Ops  |
        +-------+   +-------+ +-------+ +-------+
         60 hosts    60 hosts  60 hosts  60 hosts

Every segment must hold 60 hosts, and the design must leave room for
as many equally sized subnets as the block allows.

items.explanation: Sixty hosts need at least 62 usable addresses, which a /26 provides, and a /26 divides the /24 into four subnets, exactly matching the four segments. Option B is a /27 with only 30 usable addresses and cannot hold 60 hosts. Option D is a /28 with 14 usable and falls further short still. Option C is a /25, which does hold 126 hosts but splits the block into only two subnets, leaving two segments with nowhere to go.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which subnet does the address on GigabitEthernet0/1 belong to?

exhibit.content:
R6# show ip interface brief
Interface              IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
GigabitEthernet0/0     10.1.1.1        YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/1     172.18.45.200   YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/2     unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down

GigabitEthernet0/1 is configured with the mask 255.255.248.0.

items.explanation: A 255.255.248.0 mask is a /21, which steps in blocks of 8 in the third octet, giving boundaries at 32, 40 and 48; the address 172.18.45.200 falls in the block starting at 40 and running to 47.255. Option A treats the host's own third octet as the network number, which only holds when the mask lands on a /24. Option B picks the previous block and is the answer for anything from 172.18.32.0 to 172.18.39.255. Option D uses a block of 4, which would be a /22 rather than a /21.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which interface has been disabled by an administrator rather than failing on its own?

exhibit.content:
R7# show ip interface brief
Interface              IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
GigabitEthernet0/0     10.30.1.1       YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/1     10.30.2.1       YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/2     unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down
Loopback0              7.7.7.7         YES manual up                    up

options.text: GigabitEthernet0/0
Loopback0
GigabitEthernet0/1
GigabitEthernet0/2

items.explanation: The Status column reads administratively down only for GigabitEthernet0/2, and that wording means a shutdown command is in the configuration rather than a cable or carrier fault, which would show simply as down. Options A and C both read up in Status and Protocol and are carrying traffic normally. Option B is a loopback, which stays up because it is a virtual interface and has no physical layer to lose.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why did R8 reject the address configured on GigabitEthernet0/1?

exhibit.content:
R8(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0
R8(config-if)# ip address 10.1.0.1 255.255.0.0
R8(config-if)# exit
R8(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R8(config-if)# ip address 10.1.5.1 255.255.255.0
% 10.1.5.0 overlaps with GigabitEthernet0/0
R8(config-if)#

options.text: The mask 255.255.255.0 is invalid for an address in the 10.0.0.0 range.
10.1.5.0/24 falls inside the 10.1.0.0/16 already assigned to another interface.
A router may hold only one address from a given classful network at a time.
The second address was entered before the first interface was brought up.

items.explanation: GigabitEthernet0/0 owns 10.1.0.0 through 10.1.255.255, and 10.1.5.0/24 sits wholly inside that span, so accepting it would leave R8 with two interfaces claiming the same addresses; IOS blocks the overlap and names the conflicting interface. Option A treats the mask as illegal, but a /24 is fine in that space and the error text mentions overlap rather than the mask. Option C invents a classful limit that vanished with CIDR. Option D points at ordering, which the error message never mentions.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why can this host reach its own segment but nothing beyond it?

exhibit.content:
C:\> ipconfig

Windows IP Configuration

Ethernet adapter Ethernet:

   Connection-specific DNS Suffix  . : example.internal
   IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.30.200
   Subnet Mask . . . . . . . . . . . : 255.255.255.192
   Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.30.129

The host reaches other stations on its own segment but nothing beyond it.

options.text: The subnet mask is too long to permit traffic to leave the local segment.
The default gateway address is the broadcast address of the host's subnet.
The host address is reserved and cannot originate routed traffic.
The default gateway lies in a different subnet from the host.

items.explanation: A 255.255.255.192 mask gives blocks of 64, so the host at .200 sits in the subnet from .192 to .255 while the configured gateway at .129 sits in the block from .128 to .191; a host can only send to a gateway inside its own subnet, so off-net traffic has nowhere to go. Option A invents a mask length that blocks routing. Option B is wrong because the broadcast for this host's subnet is .255. Option C treats .200 as reserved, but it is an ordinary usable address here.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which site's block is publicly routable and therefore would not require translation at the border?

exhibit.content:
Branch address blocks proposed for a new deployment

    Site            Block
    ------------    ------------------
    Manchester      10.14.0.0/16
    Leeds           172.20.0.0/16
    Bristol         172.32.0.0/16
    Cardiff         192.168.44.0/24

All four sites reach the internet through one border router.

items.explanation: The private space in the 172 range is 172.16.0.0/12, which runs from 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255, so Bristol's 172.32.0.0/16 sits just past the end of it and is ordinary public address space. Option A falls inside 10.0.0.0/8 and is private. Option B at 172.20.0.0 sits comfortably within the /12 and is private too, which is exactly what makes the pair worth comparing. Option D falls inside 192.168.0.0/16 and is private.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why does the proposed address fail the design standard?

exhibit.content:
! R2 - proposed addressing for the new data centre
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/2
 description data centre core
 ip address 172.32.10.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
!

The design standard requires every internal segment to use address space
reserved for private use.

options.text: The private range in that space ends at 172.31.255.255.
The private range in that space ends at 172.16.255.255.
Addresses beginning 172.32 are reserved for multicast rather than unicast.
Only 10.0.0.0/8 and 192.168.0.0/16 are private; no 172 block qualifies.

items.explanation: The reserved block is 172.16.0.0/12, whose twelve network bits leave the second octet free to run from 16 through 31, so 172.32.10.1 falls one step outside private space and is publicly assigned. Option B stops the range at the end of 172.16, treating the /12 as though it were a /16 and shrinking the space sixteenfold. Option C confuses this with the multicast range, which begins at 224.0.0.0. Option D denies that any 172 block is private, which would make 172.16.0.0/12 itself public.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which entry is the shortest valid form of the recorded address?

exhibit.content:
An address has been recorded in full, unabbreviated form:

    2001:0DB8:0000:0000:0000:0AB0:0000:00CD

It must be entered into the documentation in its shortest valid form.

items.explanation: Leading zeros in a group are dropped and the single longest run of all-zero groups is replaced by a double colon, which here is the three groups before 0AB0, giving 2001:DB8::AB0:0:CD. Option A uses two double colons, which is invalid because the expansion would then be ambiguous. Option C loses a digit from 0AB0, turning it into AB and producing a different address entirely. Option D drops leading zeros correctly but never applies the double colon, so it is valid yet not the shortest form.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which global unicast address does GigabitEthernet0/0 build for itself?

exhibit.content:
! R2 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ipv6 address 2001:DB8:ACAD:1::/64 eui-64
 no shutdown
!

The burned-in address of GigabitEthernet0/0 is 001a.2b3c.4d5e.

options.text: 2001:DB8:ACAD:1:1A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E
2001:DB8:ACAD:1:21A:2BFE:FF3C:4D5E
2001:DB8:ACAD:1:21A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E
2001:DB8:ACAD:1:21A:2BFF:FE4D:5E3C

items.explanation: Modified EUI-64 splits the MAC in half, inserts FFFE between the two halves, and inverts the seventh bit of the first byte, turning 00 into 02; 001A2B and 3C4D5E therefore become 021A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E under the configured prefix. Option A skips the bit inversion and leaves the first byte as 00, which is the single commonest omission. Option B writes the inserted value as FEFF rather than FFFE. Option D transposes the final two groups of the interface identifier.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which entry correctly expresses the /64 segment for VLAN 30?

exhibit.content:
The organisation has been allocated 2001:DB8:ACAD::/48 and subnets it
into /64 segments, one per VLAN.

    VLAN 10   segment 1
    VLAN 20   segment 2
    VLAN 30   segment 7   <- being configured now

items.explanation: A /48 allocation fixes the first three groups and leaves the fourth free as a subnet identifier, so segment 7 is written 2001:DB8:ACAD:7::/64. Option B alters the third group from ACAD to ACAE, which falls outside the allocation altogether. Option C keeps the right address but labels it /48, the length of the whole allocation rather than one segment. Option D places the 7 in the interface identifier instead of the subnet field, describing a host address rather than a subnet.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which interface is up but has no address that can be routed off the local link?

exhibit.content:
R4# show ipv6 interface brief
GigabitEthernet0/0     [up/up]
    FE80::21A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E
GigabitEthernet0/1     [up/up]
    FE80::21A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5F
    2001:DB8:ACAD:9::1
GigabitEthernet0/2     [administratively down/down]
    unassigned

options.text: GigabitEthernet0/1
Loopback0
GigabitEthernet0/2
GigabitEthernet0/0

items.explanation: GigabitEthernet0/0 shows up/up but lists only an FE80 address, and link-local addresses are confined to the link they sit on, so nothing can be routed to it from elsewhere. Option A carries a 2001 global address in addition to its link-local and is fully reachable. Option C is administratively down and unassigned, so it fails the up part of the question rather than the addressing part. Option B names an interface that does not appear in this output at all.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why do the link-local pings succeed while the global ones fail?

exhibit.content:
! R1 and R2 are cabled directly to one another
!
R1  interface GigabitEthernet0/0
     ipv6 address 2001:DB8:ACAD:1::1/64
!
R2  interface GigabitEthernet0/0
     ipv6 address 2001:DB8:ACAD:2::1/64
!

Each router can ping the other's link-local address, but a ping to the
other's global address fails.

options.text: Link-local addresses are always reachable, but global addresses require DHCPv6.
The two global addresses sit in different /64 prefixes, so they need routing.
The global addresses lack an EUI-64 interface identifier and cannot be pinged.
Global addresses require ipv6 unicast-routing on both routers before any ping.

items.explanation: The fourth group differs, making the prefixes 2001:DB8:ACAD:1::/64 and 2001:DB8:ACAD:2::/64, so the two globals are on separate subnets and would need a router between them. Link-local pings still work because FE80 addresses are scoped to the shared link and do not depend on the prefixes at all, which is exactly what makes the fault look intermittent. Option A invents a DHCPv6 dependency for statically configured addresses. Option C treats EUI-64 as mandatory, but a manually written identifier is fine. Option D would prevent transit routing, not a directly connected ping.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which interface command meets the requirement?

exhibit.content:
! R6 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 no shutdown
!

GigabitEthernet0/0 must take its prefix from the router advertisements
already being sent on the segment and build its own interface identifier,
without any DHCPv6 server involved.

options.text: ipv6 address autoconfig
ipv6 address dhcp
ipv6 address 2001:DB8:ACAD:1::1/64
ipv6 enable
ipv6 unicast-routing

items.explanation: Stateless address autoconfiguration takes the prefix from a router advertisement and appends an interface identifier the device generates itself, which is precisely what the requirement describes. Option B requests an address from a DHCPv6 server, which the requirement rules out explicitly. Option C hardcodes the prefix instead of learning it, so the address would not follow a renumbering. Option D brings IPv6 up but yields a link-local address only, leaving no global address. Option E is a global command enabling forwarding for the whole router and cannot be entered against an interface.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which global unicast address has been configured on GigabitEthernet0/1?

exhibit.content:
R7# show ipv6 interface brief
GigabitEthernet0/0     [up/up]
    FE80::2D0:58FF:FE12:3401
    2001:DB8:CAFE:10::1
GigabitEthernet0/1     [up/up]
    FE80::2D0:58FF:FE12:3402
    2001:DB8:CAFE:20::1
Loopback0              [up/up]
    FE80::2D0:58FF:FE12:3400
    2001:DB8:CAFE:FF::1

options.text: 2001:DB8:CAFE:FF::1

items.explanation: Each block lists its interface first and its addresses beneath, and the second entry under GigabitEthernet0/1 is the global address 2001:DB8:CAFE:20::1. Option A belongs to GigabitEthernet0/0, the block directly above, which is the classic error of reading the right field from the neighbouring block. Option B is the correct block's link-local rather than its global address. Option D is the loopback's global address, taken from the block below.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which address is a unique local address, routable inside the organisation but never across the internet?

exhibit.content:
Addresses observed on one segment during a survey

    Host        Address
    --------    ---------------------------
    SRV-A       2001:DB8:ACAD:1::10
    SRV-B       FD3A:9C21:4E7B:1::10
    SW-MGMT     FE80::20C:29FF:FEAB:CDEF
    (group)     FF02::1

options.text: FE80::20C:29FF:FEAB:CDEF

items.explanation: Unique local addresses come from FC00::/7 and are written in practice beginning FD, so FD3A:9C21:4E7B:1::10 is the one that routes within the organisation while being filtered at its edge. Option A begins with 2001 and falls in 2000::/3, the global unicast space that is routable across the internet. Option B begins FE80 and is link-local, which cannot be routed off its own link at all. Option C begins FF and is a multicast group address rather than a unicast address for any single host.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which of the joined groups did this interface join specifically because the device is acting as a router?

exhibit.content:
R2# show ipv6 interface GigabitEthernet0/0
GigabitEthernet0/0 is up, line protocol is up
  IPv6 is enabled, link-local address is FE80::21A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E
  Global unicast address(es):
    2001:DB8:ACAD:1::1, subnet is 2001:DB8:ACAD:1::/64
  Joined group address(es):
    FF02::1
    FF02::2
    FF02::1:FF00:1
  MTU is 1500 bytes

options.text: FE80::21A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E

items.explanation: FF02::2 is the all-routers group on the local link, and only a device forwarding IPv6 joins it, so its presence marks this interface as a router's. Option A is the all-nodes group, which every IPv6 interface joins regardless of role. Option C is the solicited-node group derived from the low-order bits of the interface's own unicast address and is used for neighbour discovery by hosts and routers alike. Option D is the link-local unicast address, not a group at all.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which link-local address does this interface form for itself?

exhibit.content:
! Host NIC details
!
    Burned-in address . . . : 000c.29ab.cdef
    IPv6 routing  . . . . . : enabled on the segment

The interface has just been brought up and has not yet received a router
advertisement, so it has formed only its link-local address.

options.text: FE80::20C:29FF:FEAB:CDEF
FE80::C:29FF:FEAB:CDEF
FE80::20C:29FE:FFAB:CDEF
FE80::20C:29FF:FECD:EFAB

items.explanation: A link-local address is FE80 followed by an interface identifier built by modified EUI-64: the MAC splits into 000C29 and ABCDEF, FFFE goes between them, and the seventh bit of the first byte inverts so 00 becomes 02. Option B leaves the first byte uninverted and then drops its leading digit, losing the 02 entirely. Option C writes the inserted value as FEFF instead of FFFE. Option D rotates the final three octets of the MAC rather than keeping their order.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which address would this host use as the source when contacting a server elsewhere on the internet?

Ethernet adapter Ethernet:

Option A treats age as a tie-break, but the table stores no such preference between different prefixes. Option B assumes overlap is an error, when overlapping entries are normal and resolved by length. items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. R15 receives advertisements for 172.20.40.0/24 from both EIGRP and OSPF, and the OSPF advertisement carries a cost of 3. Why did R15 install the entry shown rather than the OSPF one?

Because the EIGRP route is internal, and internal routes are always preferred over OSPF.
Because metrics are compared only when two routes carry the same prefix length.
Because administrative distance is compared first, and EIGRP's 90 beats OSPF's 110.

items.explanation: The exhibit prints distance 90 for the EIGRP entry. When two protocols offer the same prefix, IOS compares administrative distance before it ever looks at a metric, so EIGRP wins and the OSPF cost of 3 is never weighed against 3072. Option A substitutes timing for distance. Option B invents a rule about internal routes that would apply within EIGRP, not between protocols. Option C states a condition that is already satisfied here, since both advertisements carry the same /24.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. R1 must reach every host in the 172.16.8.0 through 172.16.11.255 range by way of R2, using one static route. Which command configures it?
items.explanation: The range spans four values in the third octet, 8 through 11, which is a /22, written 255.255.252.0. Option B is a /23 and covers only 172.16.8.0 through 172.16.9.255, leaving half the range unreachable, a boundary error of exactly one block. Option C is a /24 and covers only the first quarter. Option D supplies the wildcard mask 0.0.3.255, which belongs in an access list; the ip route command expects a subnet mask.

items.explanation: A Cisco router drops IPv6 transit traffic until ipv6 unicast-routing is enabled globally; the interface still holds an address and answers pings addressed to itself, which is exactly why the fault looks like a routing problem. Option A would be required only for a link-local next hop, and this next hop is global. Option C is wrong because IOS derives a link-local address automatically. Option D confuses a host route's length with the /64 the destination network genuinely uses.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Every destination for which R3 holds no specific route must be sent to the ISP router at 203.0.113.1. Which command achieves that?

options.text: ip default-gateway 203.0.113.1
ip default-network 203.0.113.0

items.explanation: A default route is the prefix 0.0.0.0 with the mask 0.0.0.0, which matches every destination and loses every longest-match comparison, so it applies only when nothing more specific exists. Option A is a real command, but it applies to a device with IP routing disabled, such as a Layer 2 switch, and is ignored on a routing router. Option B pairs the all-zeros network with a host mask, matching only the address 0.0.0.0. Option D marks a classful network as a candidate default and does not create this route.

Option B applies a /24 mask, which IOS resolves to the whole 10.9.9.0/24 network and makes every host reachable, the opposite of the requirement. Option C supplies an all-zeros mask, producing a default-style entry rather than a host entry. Option D pairs the network address with a host mask, creating a route to 10.9.9.0 rather than to the station.

items.explanation: The IPv6 default prefix is ::/0, and static IPv6 routes are configured with the ipv6 route command, so the combination in option D is correct. Option A writes the IPv4 default prefix into an IPv6 command, mixing the two address families. Option B uses ::/128, which is the unspecified address as a host route and matches nothing useful. Option C pairs the right prefix with the IPv4 command keyword, which IOS will not accept for an IPv6 destination.

The route is refused, because Ethernet interfaces cannot appear in an ip route command.
R9 installs the route with an administrative distance of 0 rather than the usual 1.
R9 shares the traffic evenly across every other router attached to the segment.

items.explanation: Naming a broadcast interface tells R9 the destination is reachable out that port but not which neighbour to address, so it ARPs for the remote destination itself and forwards only if a neighbour answers on that host's behalf through proxy ARP. Option B is wrong because the command is accepted. Option C repeats the common belief that an exit-interface static becomes a connected route with distance 0; it still carries 1, though it is displayed as directly connected. Option D invents load sharing that no single static route performs.

Option A enables IPv4 routing, which is on by default and has no effect on IPv6 traffic. Option D points at a link-local next hop without the exit interface, which IOS rejects as ambiguous. Option E would replace the manually configured address with an autoconfigured one, changing the interface rather than establishing the route.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. R13 must reach 2001:DB8:ACAD:9::/64 through the neighbour whose link-local address is FE80::2, reached over GigabitEthernet0/0. Which command is accepted and produces that route?

Option A is a /23 and reaches only the first two subnets. Option C uses the right mask but the wrong base, covering 172.16.16.0 through 172.16.19.255, none of which are branch subnets. Option A is ruled out by the S code, which marks a static route rather than a learned one. Option B repeats the frequent belief that this display form implies distance 0; the route still carries the static default of 1. Option C describes what happens on a multi-access link, but a point-to-point serial interface has one possible receiver and uses no ARP.

Option B is a static route but a /16 network route covering 65,534 addresses. Option C is the trap: it is a /32, but its code is L, meaning IOS created it automatically for the router's own interface address rather than an administrator configuring it. items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. No router ID has been set under the OSPF process. Which value does R1 adopt as its router ID when OSPF starts?

exhibit.content:
! R1 - relevant configuration
!
interface Loopback0
 ip address 1.1.1.1 255.255.255.255
!
interface Loopback1
 ip address 9.9.9.9 255.255.255.255
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 1
 network 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
!

items.explanation: With no router-id command, OSPF prefers the highest IPv4 address on any active loopback, and 9.9.9.9 outranks 1.1.1.1. Option A assumes Loopback0 wins because of its interface number, but the comparison is on address value, not interface order. Option B is the highest physical interface address, which is consulted only when no loopback exists. Option D would mean OSPF failed to pick an ID, in which case the process refuses to start rather than running with zeros.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. An engineer sets a router ID on R2, but the verification command still reports the old value. Which action makes the configured value take effect?

exhibit.content:
R2# show ip ospf | include Routing Process
 Routing Process "ospf 1" with ID 10.1.2.1
R2#
R2# configure terminal
Enter configuration commands, one per line.  End with CNTL/Z.
R2(config)# router ospf 1
R2(config-router)# router-id 2.2.2.2

R2(config-router)# end
R2#
R2# show ip ospf | include Routing Process
 Routing Process "ospf 1" with ID 10.1.2.1

options.text: Clear the OSPF process with clear ip ospf process, or reload the router.
Re-enter the router-id command from interface configuration mode instead.
Remove and re-add the network statement so OSPF re-reads its configuration.
Configure a loopback with address 2.2.2.2 so the ID is derived from it.

items.explanation: A router ID is chosen when the OSPF process starts and is then held for the life of that process, which is why IOS prints the reload-or-clear notice visible in the exhibit. Option B invents an interface-level version of the command, which does not exist; router-id is a router-configuration command. Option C touches the network statement, which changes which interfaces run OSPF but never re-runs ID selection. Option D would matter only if no ID had been configured at all, and it still would not apply without restarting the process.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. R1 and R2 are cabled together on the 10.1.1.0/30 link, both interfaces are up, but neither lists the other as a neighbour. Which difference in the output prevents the adjacency?

options.text: Both routers report State DR, so neither will accept the other as a peer.
The hello and dead intervals differ between the two interfaces.
The two routers have different router IDs on the same segment.
The interface cost of 1 is too low for a broadcast network type.

items.explanation: Hello and dead intervals must match for two OSPF routers to become neighbours; R1 uses 10 and 40 while R2 uses 5 and 20, so the hellos are discarded and no adjacency forms. Option A misreads the symptom for the cause: both claim DR precisely because neither has seen the other, so it is a consequence. Option C inverts a requirement, since router IDs must be different rather than equal. Option D invents a minimum cost, and cost never affects whether an adjacency forms.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. The link between R1 and R2 is up and both routers run OSPF in area 0, yet no adjacency forms. What prevents it?

exhibit.content:
! R1 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 1
 router-id 1.1.1.1
 network 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
!
----------------------------------------------------------
! R2 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.5 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 2
 router-id 2.2.2.2
 network 10.1.1.4 0.0.0.3 area 0
!

options.text: The two routers have conflicting router IDs on the shared segment.
The OSPF process IDs differ, and they must match for an adjacency to form.
The hello intervals differ because only one router sets them explicitly.
The two interfaces do not sit in the same IPv4 subnet.

items.explanation: With a /30 mask, 10.1.1.1 belongs to 10.1.1.0/30 while 10.1.1.5 belongs to 10.1.1.4/30, so the addresses look adjacent but the interfaces are on different subnets and OSPF will not peer across them. Option B names the process IDs 1 and 2, which is the most tempting distractor here: the process ID is locally significant and need not match. Option A is wrong because 1.1.1.1 and 2.2.2.2 differ, which is what OSPF requires. Option C invents a timer difference neither configuration shows.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which router is elected designated router on the shared segment?

exhibit.content:
10.1.1.0/24  (broadcast segment)
      +---------+---------------+---------------+---------------+
                |               |               |               |
            +---+---+       +---+---+       +---+---+       +---+---+
            |  R1   |       |  R2   |       |  R3   |       |  R4   |
            +-------+       +-------+       +-------+       +-------+
        router-id 1.1.1.1   4.4.4.4         3.3.3.3         2.2.2.2
        ip ospf priority 1  priority 1      priority 5      priority 0

All four routers are powered on at the same moment and no adjacency
has formed yet.

options.text: R1
R2
R3
R4

items.explanation: DR election compares interface priority first and only falls back to the highest router ID on a tie. R3 carries priority 5, above every other router, so it becomes DR regardless of its router ID. Option B is the trap: R2 holds the highest router ID at 4.4.4.4 and would win only if all priorities were equal. Option A has neither the highest priority nor the highest ID. Option D is configured with priority 0, which bars it from becoming DR or BDR at all.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. R5 joins a segment where the DR and BDR were elected hours earlier. What happens to the designated router role?

exhibit.content:
10.1.1.0/24  (broadcast segment)
      +---------+---------------+---------------+---------------+
                |               |               |               |
            +---+---+       +---+---+       +---+---+       +---+---+
            |  R1   |       |  R2   |       |  R3   |       |  R5   |
            +-------+       +-------+       +-------+       +-------+
        router-id 1.1.1.1   4.4.4.4         3.3.3.3         5.5.5.5
        priority 1          priority 1      priority 5      priority 10

R3 was elected DR and R2 BDR some hours ago. R5 has just now been
cabled to the segment and brought up.

options.text: R3 stays designated router, because OSPF elections are not preemptive.
R5 becomes designated router at once, since its priority is the highest present.
R5 becomes backup designated router and is promoted at the next hello interval.
The election is rerun, making R5 designated router and R3 backup designated router.

items.explanation: OSPF elections are non-preemptive: once a DR and BDR are established, a newly arrived router with a better priority does not displace them, and R5 becomes a DROTHER until the DR fails. Option B applies the priority comparison that governs only a fresh election. Option C invents a promotion path through the BDR role, but the sitting BDR keeps its place too. Option D assumes any topology change reruns the election, which would cause exactly the churn that non-preemption exists to prevent.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. R7 must be prevented from ever becoming the designated router or backup designated router on GigabitEthernet0/0, while continuing to run OSPF there. Which command accomplishes that?

exhibit.content:
R7# show ip ospf interface brief
Interface    PID   Area            IP Address/Mask    Cost  State Nbrs F/C
Gi0/0        1     0               10.1.1.1/24        1     DR    3/3
Gi0/1        1     0               10.1.2.1/30        1     P2P   1/1

options.text: R7(config-router)# priority 0
R7(config-if)# ip ospf priority 0
R7(config-if)# ip ospf priority 255
R7(config-router)# passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/0

items.explanation: Priority is an interface setting, and the value 0 removes the router from the election while leaving OSPF running on the link. Option A has the right keyword and value but is entered in router configuration mode, where priority is not a valid command. Option C sets 255, the highest priority, which makes the router almost certain to become DR, the opposite of the requirement. Option D silences OSPF on the interface entirely, so no adjacency would form at all.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. The neighbour reached over Serial0/0/0 shows FULL with no role after the slash. What does that indicate about the link?

Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
2.2.2.2           1   FULL/BDR        00:00:36    10.1.1.2        GigabitEthernet0/0
3.3.3.3           1   FULL/DR         00:00:33    10.1.1.3        GigabitEthernet0/0

options.text: The neighbour has not finished exchanging its link-state database with R8.
The OSPF priority on that neighbour's interface has been set to zero.
The designated router for that segment has not been elected yet.
The link uses a point-to-point network type, which elects no DR or BDR.

items.explanation: OSPF elects a DR and BDR only on multi-access networks; on a point-to-point link there is no role to print, so the state shows FULL with a dash. Option A misreads FULL, which is the final state and confirms the databases are already synchronised. Option B is tempting because the Pri column reads 0, but that is what a point-to-point interface reports, not evidence of a configured priority. Option C would leave the neighbours in a transitional state rather than FULL.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which network statement enables OSPF on GigabitEthernet0/0 in area 0 without also enabling it on GigabitEthernet0/1?

exhibit.content:
! R9 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 10.1.1.65 255.255.255.192
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 1
 router-id 9.9.9.9
!

OSPF must be enabled on GigabitEthernet0/0 in area 0, and on no other
interface.

options.text: network 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
network 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 1

items.explanation: The network statement takes a wildcard mask, and a /30 corresponds to 0.0.0.3, which matches 10.1.1.0 through 10.1.1.3 and so covers GigabitEthernet0/0 alone. Option A supplies a subnet mask where the command expects a wildcard; IOS reads the value as a wildcard anyway, so the match bears no relation to the /30 link. Option B widens the match to 10.1.1.0 through 10.1.1.255, which also picks up 10.1.1.65 on GigabitEthernet0/1 and violates the requirement. Option D has the correct wildcard but places the interface in area 1, breaking the single-area design.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What is the effect of R10's configuration on the 10.1.1.0/30 link?

exhibit.content:
! R10 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 1
 router-id 10.10.10.10
 passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 network 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
!

A neighbouring router is correctly configured for area 0 on the far end
of the 10.1.1.0/30 link.

options.text: R10 advertises the 10.1.1.0/30 prefix into OSPF but forms no adjacency on that link.
R10 stops advertising 10.1.1.0/30 and forms no adjacency on that link.
R10 forms the adjacency normally but withholds the 10.1.1.0/30 prefix.
R10 is unaffected, because passive-interface applies only to distance-vector protocols.

items.explanation: A passive interface stops OSPF from sending or accepting hellos on that link, so no adjacency can form, while the network statement still causes the prefix to be advertised into the area. Option B misses that half: suppressing hellos does not withdraw the prefix. Option C reverses the behaviour entirely. Option D confuses OSPF with RIP or EIGRP, where the command exists as well; it is equally effective under OSPF, which is exactly why misapplying it silently breaks adjacencies.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which neighbour is acting as the designated router on GigabitEthernet0/0?

exhibit.content:
R11# show ip ospf neighbor

Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
5.5.5.5           1   FULL/DROTHER    00:00:31    10.1.1.5        GigabitEthernet0/0
6.6.6.6           2   FULL/DR         00:00:34    10.1.1.6        GigabitEthernet0/0
7.7.7.7           1   FULL/BDR        00:00:39    10.1.1.7        GigabitEthernet0/0

items.explanation: The State column carries the neighbour's role after the slash, and 6.6.6.6 is the row that reads FULL/DR. Option A is the DROTHER row, a neighbour that took no role in the election. Option C is the BDR, which stands by rather than serving as DR. Option D quotes an address from the Address column instead of the Neighbor ID column, which is a different field entirely and belongs to the 5.5.5.5 row.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. R1 and R2 share an up/up link but never become neighbours. Which two configuration differences account for that? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
! R1 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.252
 ip ospf hello-interval 10
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 1
 router-id 1.1.1.1
 network 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
!
----------------------------------------------------------
! R2 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.2 255.255.255.252
 ip ospf hello-interval 5
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 1
 router-id 2.2.2.2
 network 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 1
!

options.text: The two routers have been given identical router IDs.
The two interfaces have been addressed in different subnets.
The interfaces have been placed in different OSPF areas.
The configured hello intervals do not match.
One of the two interfaces has been configured as passive.

items.explanation: Two routers must agree on the area and on their hello and dead timers before an adjacency will form; R1 uses area 0 with hello 10 while R2 uses area 1 with hello 5, so both checks fail. Option A is wrong because the IDs 1.1.1.1 and 2.2.2.2 are properly distinct. Option B is wrong because 10.1.1.1 and 10.1.1.2 both sit inside 10.1.1.0/30. Option E describes a command that appears in neither configuration.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. The adjacency between R13 and its neighbour never advances beyond the state shown. Which cause does the remaining output point to?

exhibit.content:
R13# show ip ospf neighbor

Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
2.2.2.2           1   EXSTART/DR      00:00:35    10.1.1.2        GigabitEthernet0/0

R13# show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/0 | include MTU
  MTU 1500 bytes, BW 1000000 Kbit/sec, DLY 10 usec,
R13#
----------------------------------------------------------
R14# show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/0 | include MTU
  MTU 9000 bytes, BW 1000000 Kbit/sec, DLY 10 usec,

options.text: The interface MTU values on the two routers do not match.
The dead interval expired before the databases could be exchanged.
Both routers claim the designated router role for the segment.
The neighbour's router ID duplicates one already known to R13.

items.explanation: An adjacency that halts at EXSTART or EXCHANGE points at the database exchange itself, and the two interfaces report 1500 and 9000 bytes, so the routers cannot agree on a payload size and the exchange never completes. Option B is wrong because an expired dead interval drops the neighbour out of the table rather than freezing it in EXSTART. Option C describes a condition that resolves through election rather than stalling the exchange. Option D would prevent the neighbour from being listed at all rather than holding it mid-exchange.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. The OSPF process on R14 carries no network statements, and the design calls for enabling OSPF directly on the interface instead. Which command does that?

exhibit.content:
! R14 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 1
 router-id 14.14.14.14
!

options.text: R14(config-router)# network GigabitEthernet0/0 area 0
R14(config-if)# ip ospf 1 area 0
R14(config-if)# ospf 1 area 0
R14(config-router)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0 area 0

items.explanation: The interface-level form is ip ospf followed by the process ID and the area, entered under the interface, and it enables OSPF on that interface without any network statement. Option A keeps the network keyword, which expects an address and wildcard rather than an interface name. Option C drops the leading ip, so IOS does not recognise the command. Option D tries to nest an interface command inside router configuration mode, mixing the two modes that the interface-level form exists to separate.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What OSPF cost does R15 assign to Serial0/0/0?

exhibit.content:
R15# show interfaces Serial0/0/0 | include BW
  MTU 1500 bytes, BW 1544 Kbit/sec, DLY 20000 usec,
R15#
R15# show ip ospf | include Reference bandwidth
 Reference bandwidth unit is 100 mbps

items.explanation: Cost is the reference bandwidth divided by interface bandwidth, so 100,000,000 divided by 1,544,000 gives 64.77, and OSPF discards the remainder to leave 64. Option C rounds the quotient up to 65 instead of truncating, which is the single commonest arithmetic slip on this calculation. Option A is the cost a link at or above the reference bandwidth receives, since the formula floors at 1. Option B quotes the reference bandwidth itself rather than the result of the division.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. The neighbour has been sitting in the state shown for several minutes. What does that state indicate?

Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
2.2.2.2           1   INIT/DROTHER    00:00:31    10.1.1.2        GigabitEthernet0/0

options.text: The neighbour finished exchanging databases but has not installed the routes.
R17 has seen the neighbour's hello, but the neighbour has not yet seen R17's.
The two routers disagree over which of them is the designated router.
The dead interval has expired and the neighbour is being removed from the table.

items.explanation: INIT means hellos are arriving in one direction only: R17 has heard the neighbour, but has not yet seen its own router ID listed in the neighbour's hello, so the relationship cannot advance to two-way. It usually points at something filtering traffic in one direction. Option A describes FULL, the state that follows a completed exchange. Option C describes an election dispute, which does not hold a neighbour at INIT. Option D is contradicted by the Dead Time of 31 seconds still counting down.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which OSPF cost does R18 apply to traffic leaving Serial0/0/0?

Option A takes the cost from the GigabitEthernet0/0 row, reading the right column on the wrong line. Option B quotes 110, which is OSPF's administrative distance and never appears in this output at all. Option D assumes an unlisted interface costs nothing, but every OSPF-enabled interface carries a cost of at least 1.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Both ends of this Ethernet link have been set to the point-to-point network type. What will show ip ospf neighbor report once the adjacency settles?

options.text: A designated router and backup are still elected, but the hello timers halve.
No adjacency forms, because Ethernet interfaces cannot use that network type.
The adjacency reaches FULL, but no link-state advertisements cross the link.
No designated router is elected, and the state shows FULL with no role.

items.explanation: Changing the network type to point-to-point tells OSPF to treat the segment as having exactly two routers, so the election is skipped entirely and the neighbour prints as FULL with a dash where a role would otherwise appear. Option A keeps an election that the network type removes. Option B assumes the type is tied to the physical medium, but it is a software setting commonly applied to Ethernet links carrying only two routers. Option C would leave the routers with no shared topology, which FULL rules out.

options.text: The wildcard mask in the network statement forced the advertised length to /32.
OSPF summarised the loopback prefix to its classful boundary before advertising.
OSPF advertises a loopback as a host route unless the network type is changed.
R21 applied its own mask, because the two routers sit in different areas.

items.explanation: OSPF treats a loopback as a stub host and advertises it as a /32 no matter what mask the interface carries, which is why R21 installs 10.9.9.9/32; setting the interface to the point-to-point network type is what restores the configured length. Option A confuses the wildcard, which selects which interfaces participate, with the length that gets advertised. Option B describes summarisation to a classful boundary, which would produce a shorter prefix rather than a longer one. Option D invokes an area difference that the single-area configuration rules out.

items.explanation: Hosts point at the virtual address the group presents, listed in the Virtual IP column as 10.1.1.1, which survives a failover because the standby router adopts it. Option A is R1's own interface address, and pointing hosts there would strand them the moment R1 failed, which is the entire problem an FHRP exists to solve. Option B is the standby router's real address and has the same weakness. Option D reads the Pri column value of 110 as though it were part of an address.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which virtual MAC address does R2 use for this HSRP group?

exhibit.content:
! R2 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.2 255.255.255.0
 standby version 1
 standby 10 ip 10.1.1.1
 standby 10 priority 110
 standby 10 preempt
!

items.explanation: An HSRP version 1 virtual MAC is 0000.0C07.AC followed by the group number in hexadecimal, and group 10 in hex is 0a, giving 0000.0c07.ac0a. Option A writes the group as the literal digits 10, producing 0000.0c07.ac10, which is a genuine virtual MAC but belongs to group 16. Option C uses the 0000.5E00.01 range, which identifies VRRP rather than HSRP. Option D is the group 1 address, ignoring the configured group number entirely.

options.text: R2 stays active and R1 becomes standby, despite R1's higher priority.
R1 resumes the active role at once, because its priority is the higher of the two.
Both routers hold the active role until the next hello exchange separates them.
R1 stays out of the group until preemption is configured on R2.

items.explanation: Priority decides an election, but without the preempt keyword a returning router cannot displace a sitting active router, so R2 keeps the role and R1 settles for standby. Option B applies the priority comparison to a group that has already elected, which is what preemption exists to enable and neither router has it. Option C describes a split-active state that the hello exchange prevents. Option D inverts the requirement: preemption would be needed on R1, the router trying to take over, not on R2.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What does PC1 experience after R1 loses power?

options.text: PC1 must be reconfigured with R2's interface address as its gateway.
PC1 has to renew its DHCP lease to be issued a new default gateway.
PC1 loses reachability until its ARP cache expires and it re-resolves.
PC1 keeps the same gateway, as R2 takes over the virtual IP and MAC.

items.explanation: The standby router assumes both the virtual IP address and the virtual MAC address, so the entry already cached by PC1 stays valid and forwarding resumes without any change on the host. That property is the whole purpose of a first hop redundancy protocol. Option A would require touching every host, which is precisely what the protocol avoids. Option B assumes a DHCP dependency PC1 does not have, since its gateway is static. Option C is the most tempting error: it would be true if only the IP moved, but the virtual MAC moves with it.

          standby 1 priority 90    standby 1 priority 120
          standby 1 preempt        standby 1 preempt

Both routers use virtual IP 10.1.1.1 in HSRP group 1 and are
brought up at the same time.

options.text: R1, because it holds the lower interface address on the segment.
Both routers share the load, since each is configured to preempt.
R2, because its configured priority is the higher of the two.
Whichever router completed boot first and claimed the virtual address.

items.explanation: HSRP elects the router with the numerically higher priority, so R2's 120 beats R1's 90 and R2 becomes active while R1 stands by. Option A applies a lowest-address tie-break, which HSRP consults only when priorities are equal, and even then it prefers the higher address. Option B assumes load sharing between the two, but a single HSRP group has exactly one forwarder. Option D describes what would happen without preemption, yet both routers carry the preempt keyword, so the higher priority asserts itself regardless of boot order.

options.text: R6's priority falls to 90, and the router at 10.1.1.3 preempts to become active.
R6's priority falls to 90, but R6 stays active because it already owns the role.
R6 leaves the group entirely and stops responding to the virtual IP address.

items.explanation: The tracking statement decrements R6's priority by 20 when the object goes down, taking 110 to 90, which is below the standby router's 100; because both routers are configured to preempt, the router at 10.1.1.3 then takes the active role. Option B ignores preemption, which is exactly what makes the decrement useful. Option C overstates the effect, as a lowered priority demotes the router rather than removing it. items.explanation: An ARP request for the virtual IP is answered with the group's virtual MAC, 0000.0c07.ac01, which is why the cached entry stays correct after a failover moves the role to the other router. Option A is R8's burned-in address; a host that cached it would lose reachability the moment R8 failed, defeating the redundancy. Option C is R9's burned-in address and has the same flaw. Option D is the broadcast address, which never appears as the resolved result of an ARP request.

options.text: The routers negotiate a single group and elect R1 as the active router.
Each router becomes the active router for its own group.
Both routers answer ARP for 10.1.1.1 with different virtual MACs.
Neither router responds to traffic addressed to 10.1.1.1.
R1 suppresses R2's group because it holds the higher configured priority.

items.explanation: HSRP routers only negotiate with peers in the same group number, so R1 in group 1 and R2 in group 2 never see each other; each declares itself active for its own group, and each answers for 10.1.1.1 with the virtual MAC derived from its own group number. Option A assumes the shared virtual IP is enough to pair them, when the group number is what binds peers. Option D contradicts both routers being active. Option E applies a priority comparison across groups that never communicate.
